claim: Spatial hearing in cochlear implant (CI) patients remains a major challenge, with many early deaf users reported to have no measurable sensitivity to interaural time differences (ITDs).
source: Spatial hearing in cochlear implant (CI) patients remains a major challenge, with many early deaf users reported to have no measurable sensitivity to interaural time differences (ITDs).
evidence: This claim is supported by references to existing literature on CI patient outcomes.

claim: Deprivation of binaural experience during an early critical period is often hypothesized to be the cause of poor ITD sensitivity in early deaf CI users.
source: Deprivation of binaural experience during an early critical period is often hypothesized to be the cause of this shortcoming.
evidence: This represents a hypothesis commonly found in the literature about critical periods.

claim: Neonatally deafened (ND) rats provided with precisely synchronized CI stimulation in adulthood can be trained to lateralize ITDs with behavioral thresholds near 50 μs.
source: However, we show that neonatally deafened (ND) rats provided with precisely synchronized CI stimulation in adulthood can be trained to lateralize ITDs with essentially normal behavioral thresholds near 50 μs.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by behavioral experimental data presented in Figure 2.

claim: Neonatally deafened rats show high physiological sensitivity to ITDs immediately after binaural implantation in adulthood.
source: Furthermore, comparable ND rats show high physiological sensitivity to ITDs immediately after binaural implantation in adulthood.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings from the inferior colliculus presented in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: The good ITD thresholds achieved by ND-CI rats raise questions about whether shortcomings in technology or treatment, rather than missing input during early development, may be behind poor binaural outcomes for current CI patients.
source: Our result that ND-CI rats achieved very good behavioral ITD thresholds, while prelingually deaf human CI patients often fail to develop a useful sensitivity to ITD raises urgent questions concerning the possibility that shortcomings in technology or treatment, rather than missing input during early development, may be behind the usually poor binaural outcomes for current CI patients.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparing the experimental results with known clinical outcomes.

claim: Cochlear implants can be enormously beneficial for patients with severe to profound sensorineural hearing loss, particularly when CI implantation takes place early in life.
source: For patients with severe to profound sensorineural hearing loss, cochlear implants (CIs) can be enormously beneficial, as they often permit spoken language acquisition, particularly when CI implantation takes place early in life (Kral and Sharma, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kral and Sharma, 2012.

claim: The auditory performance achieved by CI users remains variable and falls short of natural hearing.
source: Nevertheless, the auditory performance achieved by CI users remains variable and falls a long way short of natural hearing.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of cochlear implant research.

claim: Good speech understanding in the presence of competing sound sources requires the ability to separate speech from background, which is aided by spatial release from masking.
source: For example, good speech understanding in the presence of competing sound sources requires the ability to separate speech from background. This is aided by 'spatial release from masking', a binaural phenomenon, which relies on the brain's ability to process binaural spatial cues, including interaural level and time differences (ILDs and ITDs) (Ellinger et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Ellinger et al., 2017 and represents established knowledge.

claim: Bilateral cochlear implantation is becoming more common.
source: While bilateral cochlear implantation is becoming more common (Litovsky, 2010; Conti-Ramsden et al., 2012; Ehlers et al., 2017)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations documenting the trend.

claim: Bilateral CI recipients perform poorly in binaural tasks such as sound localization and auditory scene analysis, particularly when multiple sound sources are present.
source: bilateral CI recipients still perform poorly in binaural tasks such as sound localization and auditory scene analysis, particularly when multiple sound sources are present (van Hoesel, 2004; van Hoesel, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to van Hoesel, 2004 and van Hoesel, 2012.

claim: Normal hearing human listeners may be able to detect ITDs as small as 10 μs.
source: Indeed, while normal hearing (NH) human listeners may be able to detect ITDs as small as 10 μs (Zwislocki and Feldman, 1956)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Zwislocki and Feldman, 1956.

claim: ITD sensitivity of CI patients, particularly with prelingual onset of deafness, is often poor and sometimes seems completely absent.
source: ITD sensitivity of CI patients, particularly with prelingual onset of deafness, is often poor and sometimes seems completely absent (van Hoesel, 2004; Litovsky, 2010; van Hoesel, 2012; Kerber and Seeber, 2012; Litovsky et al., 2012; Laback et al., 2015; Ehlers et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations documenting poor ITD sensitivity in prelingually deaf CI patients.

claim: Two main factors are generally thought to be chiefly responsible for poor binaural sensitivity of CI recipients: technical limitations of current CI devices and neurobiological factors.
source: The reasons for the poor binaural sensitivity of CI recipients are only poorly understood, but two main factors are generally thought to be chiefly responsible, namely: (1) technical limitations of current CI devices and (2) neurobiological factors, such as when the neural circuitry responsible for processing binaural cues fails to develop due to a lack of experience during a presumed 'critical period' in early life or when it degenerates during a period of late deafness.
evidence: This represents the prevailing hypotheses in the field.

claim: The vast majority of CI devices in clinical use operate stimulation which are variants of the 'continuous interleaved sampling' (CIS) method.
source: The vast majority of CI devices in clinical use operate stimulation, which are variants of the 'continuous interleaved sampling' (CIS) method (Wilson et al., 1991).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wilson et al., 1991 and represents established knowledge about CI technology.

claim: Many postlingually deaf CI users show better ITD sensitivity when tested with experimental processors, with some achieving thresholds comparable to those seen in NH peers.
source: When tested with such experimental devices, many postlingually deaf CI users show better ITD sensitivity, with some of the best performers achieving thresholds comparable to those seen in NH peers.
evidence: This is based on established findings in the literature about postlingually deaf CI users.

claim: The ITD performance of prelingually deaf CI users remains invariably poor, with even rare star performers only achieving thresholds of a few hundred microseconds.
source: In contrast, the ITD performance of prelingually deaf CI users remains invariably poor, with even rare star performers only achieving thresholds of a few hundred microsecond (Poon et al., 2009; Conti-Ramsden et al., 2012; Litovsky et al., 2012; Gordon et al., 2014; Laback et al., 2015; Litovsky and Gordon, 2016; Ehlers et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations documenting poor ITD performance in prelingually deaf CI users.

claim: The poor performance of prelingually deaf patients even under optimized experimental conditions led to the suggestion that the absence of binaural inputs during a presumed 'critical' period in early childhood may prevent the development of ITD sensitivity.
source: It is this poor performance of prelingually deaf patients even under optimized experimental conditions that led to the suggestion that the absence of binaural inputs during a presumed 'critical' period in early childhood may prevent the development of ITD sensitivity (Kral and Sharma, 2012; Kral, 2013; Litovsky and Gordon, 2016; Yusuf et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies proposing the critical period hypothesis.

claim: Amblyopia is an example of a strong critical period disorder where patients experience uneven or unbalanced binocular visual stimulation in early life, leading to failure of normal development of the brain's binocular circuitry.
source: Perhaps the best studied example of a strong critical period disorder is amblyopia. Amblyopic patients experience an uneven or unbalanced binocular visual stimulation in early life, which leads to a failure of the normal development of the brain's binocular circuitry.
evidence: This is established knowledge about amblyopia as a critical period disorder.

claim: Amblyopia causes impairments in visual acuity in the 'weaker eye' and in stereoscopic vision that can only be fully reversed if diagnosed and treated prior to critical period closure.
source: This, in turn, causes sometimes dramatic impairments in the visual acuity in the 'weaker eye', as well as in stereoscopic vision. These impairments can only be fully reversed if diagnosed and treated prior to critical period closure, and despite substantial research efforts, no interventions performed after critical period closure can offer more than partial remediation of the deficits (Tsirlin et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tsirlin et al., 2015 and represents established knowledge about amblyopia treatment.

claim: For neonatally deaf patients, periods of sensory deprivation during development are the norm because profound bilateral hearing loss is hard to diagnose in neonates.
source: For neonatally deaf patients, periods of sensory deprivation during development are the norm because profound bilateral hearing loss is hard to diagnose in neonates and measurements of auditory brainstem responses (ABRs) have to be repeated to exclude delayed maturation of the auditory brainstem (Jöhr et al., 2008; Cosetti and Roland, 2010; Arndt et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations documenting challenges in early diagnosis of hearing loss.

claim: Risks associated with anesthesia in young babies provide a disincentive for very early implantation.
source: Finally, risks associated with anesthesia in young babies provide another disincentive for very early implantation (Dettman et al., 2007; Jöhr et al., 2008; Cosetti and Roland, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations documenting anesthesia risks in infants.

claim: By the time of implantation, neonatally deaf pediatric CI patients will typically already have missed out on many months of auditory input.
source: Altogether, this means by the time of implantation, neonatally deaf pediatric CI patients will typically already have missed out on many months of the auditory input.
evidence: This is an inference based on the previously stated facts about delays in diagnosis and treatment.

claim: Immunohistochemical studies have shown degraded tonotopic organization in neonatally deafened CI rats.
source: Various lines of animal experimentation make such a critical period hypothesis plausible, including immunohistochemical studies that have shown degraded tonotopic organization (Rosskothen-Kuhl and Illing, 2012; Rauch et al., 2016)
evidence: This is supported by citations to immunohistochemical studies.

claim: Neonatally deafened CI rats show changes in stimulation-induced molecular, cellular, and morphological properties of the auditory pathway.
source: and changes in stimulation-induced molecular, cellular, and morphological properties of the auditory pathway of neonatally deafened (ND) CI rats (Illing and Rosskothen-Kuhl, 2012; Rosskothen-Kuhl and Illing, 2012; Jakob et al., 2015; Rauch et al., 2016; Rosskothen-Kuhl et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations documenting changes in the auditory pathway.

claim: Abnormal sensory input during early development can alter ITD tuning curves in key brainstem nuclei of gerbils.
source: Additional studies demonstrate that abnormal sensory input during early development can alter ITD tuning curves in key brainstem nuclei of gerbils (Seidl and Grothe, 2005; Beiderbeck et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies in gerbils.

claim: Electrophysiological studies on cats and rabbits have reported significantly lower ITD sensitivity to CI stimulation in the inferior colliculus after early deafening compared to hearing experienced controls.
source: Furthermore, numerous electrophysiological studies on cats and rabbits have reported significantly lower ITD sensitivity to CI stimulation in the inferior colliculus (IC) (Hancock et al., 2010; Hancock et al., 2012; Hancock et al., 2013; Chung et al., 2019) and auditory cortex (AC) (Tillein et al., 2010; Tillein et al., 2016) after early deafening compared to what is observed in hearing experienced controls.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to electrophysiological studies in cats and rabbits.

claim: The 'strong critical period hypothesis' of poor ITD sensitivity in CI patients has not yet been rigorously tested.
source: However, although the 'strong critical period hypothesis' of poor ITD sensitivity in CI patients is plausible, it has not yet been rigorously tested.
evidence: This is an assessment of the state of the literature.

claim: Previous animal studies have not investigated perceptual limits of binaural function in behavioral experiments using optimized binaural inputs.
source: The previous animal studies just mentioned have not investigated perceptual limits of binaural function in behavioral experiments using optimized binaural inputs.
evidence: This is an assessment of limitations in previous studies.

claim: CI patients with NH experience in early childhood usually have better ITD sensitivity than patients without.
source: Similarly, while we do know that CI patients with NH experience in early childhood usually have a better ITD sensitivity than patients without (Litovsky, 2010; Laback et al., 2015; Ehlers et al., 2017)
evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical studies.

claim: It is unknown whether early deaf patients could develop good ITD sensitivity after implantation later in life if fitted with CI processors providing optimized binaural stimulation from the outset.
source: we do not yet know whether early deaf patients could develop good ITD sensitivity after implantation later in life if they were fitted with CI processors providing with optimized binaural stimulation from the outset.
evidence: This identifies a gap in current knowledge.

claim: Only research interfaces that are unsuitable for everyday clinical use can deliver the high-quality binaural inputs needed to investigate ITD sensitivity in early deaf CI patients.
source: Currently, only research interfaces that are unsuitable for everyday clinical use can deliver the high-quality binaural inputs needed to investigate this question.
evidence: This is a statement about current technological limitations.

claim: There are currently no patient cohorts who experienced through their CIs the long periods of high-quality ITD information that may be needed for them to become expert at using ITDs.
source: Consequently, there are currently no patient cohorts who experienced through their CIs the long periods of high-quality ITD information that may be needed for them to become expert at using ITDs, irrespective of any hypothetical critical periods.
evidence: This is an inference based on the limitations of current CI technology and clinical practice.

claim: The innate ability of the ND auditory pathway to encode ITD may atrophy after prolonged exposure to binaural CI stimulation through conventional clinical processors which convey no useful ITD information.
source: We cannot at present exclude the possibility that the ND auditory pathway may retain a substantial innate ability to encode ITD even after long periods of neonatal deafness, but that this ability may atrophy after countless hours of binaural CI stimulation through conventional clinical processors which convey no useful ITD information.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis proposed by the authors.

claim: Five ND rats that received chronic bilateral CIs in young adulthood were trained in a two-alternative forced choice ITD lateralization task.
source: To test whether ND rats can learn to discriminate ITDs of CI stimuli, we trained five ND rats that received chronic bilateral CIs in young adulthood (postnatal weeks 10–14) in a two-alternative forced choice (2AFC) ITD lateralization task (NDCI-B; see Figure 1)
evidence: This describes the experimental design and is supported by the data presented.

claim: The performance of NDCI-B rats was compared against behavioral data from five age-matched NH rats trained to discriminate the ITDs of acoustic pulse trains.
source: and we compared their performance against behavioral data from five age-matched NH rats trained to discriminate the ITDs of acoustic pulse trains (NH-B; see Figure 1; Li et al., 2019).
evidence: This describes the experimental design with a control group.

claim: Animals initiated trials by licking a center 'start spout' and responded to 200 ms long 50 Hz binaural pulse trains by licking either a left or a right 'response spout' to receive drinking water as positive reinforcement.
source: Animals initiated trials by licking a center 'start spout' and responded to 200 ms long 50 Hz binaural pulse trains by licking either a left or a right 'response spout' to receive drinking water as positive reinforcement (Figure 2—figure supplements 1a and 2b; Video 1).
evidence: This describes the behavioral task methodology, supported by figures and video.

claim: NDCI-B rats were stimulated with biphasic electrical pulse trains delivered through chronic CIs, while NH-B rats received acoustic pulse trains through near-field sound tubes.
source: NDCI-B rats were stimulated with biphasic electrical pulse trains delivered through chronic CIs, NH-B rats received acoustic pulse trains through a pair of 'open stereo headphones' implemented as near-field sound tubes positioned next to each ear when the animal was at the start spout (Figure 2—figure supplements 2a, see Li et al., 2019 for details).
evidence: This describes the stimulation methods for both groups.

claim: Systematic ITD differences were the only reliable cue available to the rats during testing.
source: We used pulses of identical amplitude in each ear, so that systematic ITD differences were the only reliable cue available (Figure 2—figure supplements 1c,d and 2f).
evidence: This describes the experimental control to isolate ITD as the relevant cue.

claim: The behavioral data were collected over a testing period of around 14 days.
source: The behavioral data (Figure 2) were collected over a testing period of around 14 days.
evidence: This describes the duration of data collection.

claim: For NDCI-B rats, the initial lateralization training started usually 1 day after CI implantation.
source: For NDCI-B rats, the initial lateralization training started usually 1 day after CI implantation.
evidence: This describes the timing of behavioral training relative to implantation.

claim: On average, rats were trained for 8 days before testing on ITD sensitivity began.
source: On average, rats were trained for 8 days before we started to test them on ITD sensitivity.
evidence: This describes the training duration before formal testing.

claim: All rats, whether NH with acoustic stimulation or ND with CI stimulation, were capable of lateralizing ITDs.
source: Figure 2 clearly demonstrates that all rats, whether NH with acoustic stimulation or ND with CI stimulation, were capable of lateralizing ITDs.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by the behavioral data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The observed mean ITD sensitivity for the NDCI-B animals (0.487%/µs) is only about 20% worse than that of the NH-B animals (0.657%/µs).
source: Remarkably, the observed mean sensitivity for the NDCI-B animals (0.487%/µs) is only about 20% worse than that of the NH-B (0.657%/µs).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of behavioral performance between groups, derived from data in Figure 2.

claim: The differences in mean ITD sensitivity between NDCI-B and NH-B groups were not statistically significant (p=0.4375, Wilcoxon test).
source: Indeed, we performed a Wilcoxon test on the slopes and found no significant difference (p=0.4375).
evidence: This is a statistical analysis of the behavioral data.

claim: Both NDCI-B and NH-B cohorts showed similar 75% correct lateralization thresholds (median NH-B: 41.5 µs; median NDCI-B: 54.8 µs; mean NH-B: 79.9 µs; mean NDCI-B: 63.5 µs).
source: Similarly, both cohorts showed similar 75% correct lateralization thresholds (median NH-B: 41.5 µs; median NDCI-B: 54.8 µs; mean NH-B: 79.9 µs; mean NDCI-B: 63.5 µs).
evidence: This is a quantitative summary of behavioral thresholds from the data.

claim: The ITD thresholds of ND-CI rats are orders of magnitude better than those reported for prelingually deaf human CI patients, who often have ITD thresholds in excess of 3000 µs.
source: Remarkably, the ITD thresholds of our ND-CI rats are thus orders of magnitude better than those reported for prelingually deaf human CI patients, who often have ITD thresholds too large to measure and often in excess of 3000 µs (Litovsky et al., 2010; Ehlers et al., 2017).
evidence: This compares the experimental results with published data on human CI patients.

claim: Thresholds in ND rats were not dissimilar from the approx. 10–60 µs range of 75% correct ITD discrimination thresholds reported for normal human subjects tested with noise bursts and pure tones.
source: Thresholds in ND rats were not dissimilar from the approx. 10–60 µs range of 75% correct ITD discrimination thresholds reported for normal human subjects tested with noise bursts (Klumpp and Eady, 1956), and pure tones (Zwislocki and Feldman, 1956)
evidence: This compares the experimental results with published data on normal human hearing.

claim: Thresholds in ND rats were similar to the ≈40 µs thresholds reported for NH ferrets tested with noise bursts.
source: or the ≈40 µs thresholds reported for NH ferrets tested with noise bursts (Keating et al., 2013a).
evidence: This compares the experimental results with published data on ferrets.

claim: Responses of n = 1140 multi-units were recorded in the IC of four young adult ND rats (NDCI-E).
source: To investigate the amount of physiological ITD sensitivity present in the hearing inexperienced rat brain, we recorded responses of n = 1140 multi-units in the IC of four young adult ND rats (NDCI-E; see Figures 1 and 3).
evidence: This describes the electrophysiology experiment sample size and methods.

claim: NDCI-E rats were stimulated by isolated, bilateral CI pulses with ITDs varying randomly over a ±160 μs range.
source: These rats were litter mates of the behavioral ND animals (NDCI-B) and were stimulated by isolated, bilateral CI pulses with ITDs varying randomly over a ±160 μs range (ca 123% of the rat's physiological range Koka et al., 2008).
evidence: This describes the stimulation protocol for electrophysiology experiments.

claim: For the NDCI-E cohort, the CI implantation and the electrophysiology measurements in the IC were performed on the same day with no prior electric hearing experience.
source: For the cohort of neonatally deafened rats (NDCI-E), the CI implantation and the electrophysiology measurements in the IC were performed on the same day with no prior electric hearing experience.
evidence: This describes the timing of electrophysiology relative to implantation.

claim: Responses of IC neurons in NDCI-E rats were detected for currents as low as 100 μA.
source: Responses of IC neurons were detected for currents as low as 100 μA.
evidence: This describes the threshold for neural responses in the electrophysiology experiments.

claim: ITD tuning in NDCI-E animals varied from one recording site to the next both in shape and magnitude, and firing rates clearly varied as a function of ITD values.
source: For NDCI-E animals, ITD tuning varied from one recording site to the next both in shape and magnitude and firing rates clearly varied as a function of ITD values (Figure 3).
evidence: This describes the variability in neural responses observed in the electrophysiology data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Many multi-units in NDCI-E rats showed typical short-latency onset responses to the stimulus with varying response amplitudes.
source: While many multi-units showed typical short-latency onset responses to the stimulus with varying response amplitudes (Figure 3, #1, #3)
evidence: This describes a pattern observed in the electrophysiology data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Some multi-units in NDCI-E rats showed sustained, but still clearly tuned, responses extending for up to 80 ms or longer post-stimulus.
source: some showed sustained, but still clearly tuned, responses extending for up to 80 ms or longer post-stimulus (Figure 3, #4).
evidence: This describes another pattern observed in the electrophysiology data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The shapes of ITD tuning curves observed in rat IC resembled mostly the 'peak', 'monotonic sigmoid', 'trough', and 'multi-peak' shapes previously described in the IC of cats.
source: Although the interpretation of tuning curves is complex the shapes of ITD tuning curves we observed in rat IC (Figure 3) resembled mostly the 'peak', 'monotonic sigmoid', 'trough', and 'multi-peak' shapes previously described in the IC of cats (Smith and Delgutte, 2007).
evidence: This compares the observed tuning curve shapes with those reported in the literature.

claim: The median STVR value for IC multi-units in NDCI-E rats was 0.362.
source: It is noticeable that the proportion of multi-units with relatively large STVRs values (substantial ITD tuning) is high among the NDCI-E rats with a median STVR value for IC multi-units of 0.362.
evidence: This is a quantitative summary of the ITD sensitivity in the electrophysiology data.

claim: Hancock et al., 2010 showed a lower median STVR (referred to as SNR) for congenitally deaf cats (0.19) compared to adult deafened cats (0.45).
source: In comparison, Hancock et al., 2010 showed a lower median STVR (referred to as SNR) for congenitally deaf cats (0.19) as compared to adult deafened cats (0.45).
evidence: This cites quantitative data from a previous study for comparison.

claim: The proportion of rat multi-units that showed statistically significant ITD tuning (p≤0.01) was approximately 91% (1125/1229) in ND CI-stimulated rats.
source: The proportion of rat multi-units that showed statistically significant ITD tuning (p≤0.01), as determined by ANOVA (see Materials and methods), was also very large in ND (1125/1229 ≈ 91%) CI-stimulated rats.
evidence: This is a quantitative summary of the proportion of ITD-sensitive units in the electrophysiology data.

claim: For rats that were deafened before the onset of hearing, a lack of early auditory experience during what ought to have been a critical period for ITD sensitivity did not produce a measurable decline in overall sensitivity of IC neurons to the ITD of CI stimulus pulses.
source: Thus, for our rats that were deafened before the onset of hearing, a lack of early auditory experience during what ought to have been a critical period for ITD sensitivity did not produce a measurable decline in overall sensitivity of IC neurons to the ITD of CI stimulus pulses.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the electrophysiology results.

claim: Previous studies comparing ITD tuning in the IC of congenitally deaf white cats with that of hearing experienced, adult deafened wild type cats reported noticeably worse ITD tuning in the congenitally deaf cats.
source: This is perhaps unexpected given that previous studies comparing ITD tuning in the IC of congenitally deaf white cats with that of hearing experienced, adult deafened wild type cats did report noticeably worse ITD tuning in the congenitally deaf cats (Hancock et al., 2013).
evidence: This cites previous findings for comparison with the current results.

claim: Congenitally deaf white cats lose hair-cell function between postnatal days 3 and 10.
source: Note that congenitally deaf white cats lose hair-cell function between postnatal days 3 and 10 (Mair and Elverland, 1977).
evidence: This is a citation to a previous study describing the timing of deafness in congenitally deaf cats.

claim: Many IC neurons in the inexperienced, adult midbrain of NDCI-E rats are quite sensitive to changes in ITD of CI pulse stimuli by just a few tens of microseconds.
source: Nevertheless, the results in Figures 3 and 4 clearly show that many IC neurons in the inexperienced, adult midbrain of NDCI-E rats are quite sensitive to changes in ITD of CI pulse stimuli by just a few tens of microsecond
evidence: This is a summary of the electrophysiology findings shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: NDCI-B rats can readily learn to use neural ITD sensitivity to perform behavioral ITD discrimination with an accuracy similar to that seen in their NH-B litter mates.
source: and our behavioral experiments showed that NDCI-B rats (Figure 2f–j) can readily learn to use this neural sensitivity to perform behavioral ITD discrimination with an accuracy similar to that seen in their NH-B litter mates (Figure 2a–e).
evidence: This connects the electrophysiology and behavioral findings.

claim: This study is the first demonstration that, at least in rats, severely degraded auditory experience in early development does not inevitably lead to impaired binaural time processing in adulthood.
source: This study is the first demonstration that, at least in rats, severely degraded auditory experience in early development does not inevitably lead to impaired binaural time processing in adulthood.
evidence: This is a summary claim about the novelty and significance of the study.

claim: Some studies deemed rats to be a poor model for ITD processing due to medial superior olives with less ITD-sensitive neurons and their limited low-frequency hearing.
source: First, some studies deemed rats to be a poor model for ITD processing due to medial superior olives (MSOs) with less ITD-sensitive neurons and their limited low-frequency hearing that may result in limited ITD perception (Grothe and Klump, 2000; Wesolek et al., 2010).
evidence: This cites previous concerns about using rats as a model for ITD processing.

claim: In animals with relatively high-frequency hearing, such as rats, envelope ITD coding through the lateral superior olive is likely to make important contributions.
source: However, in animals with relatively high-frequency hearing, such as rats, envelope ITD coding through the lateral superior olive is likely to make important contributions (Joris and Yin, 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citation and represents established knowledge about ITD processing mechanisms.

claim: A previous behavioral study of ITD sensitivity in rats concluded that rats are unlikely to be sensitive to the interaural phase of relatively low-frequency tones.
source: The only previous behavioral study of ITD sensitivity in rats outside of our lab (Wesolek et al., 2010) concluded that rats are unlikely to be sensitive to the interaural phase of relatively low-frequency tones.
evidence: This cites a previous study's conclusion about rat ITD sensitivity.

claim: High-frequency 'envelope' ITD sensitivity is likely to be of great importance in prosthetic hearing given that CIs rarely reach the apex of the cochlea.
source: High-frequency 'envelope' ITD sensitivity is also bound to be of great importance in prosthetic hearing given that CIs rarely reach the apex of the cochlea.
evidence: This is an inference based on the anatomy of CI placement and the frequency regions they stimulate.

claim: Li et al., 2019 demonstrated that NH rats can use ITD cues for 2AFC sound lateralization tasks and show ITD sensitivity to broadband clicks.
source: In Li et al., 2019, we recently demonstrate that NH rats can use ITD cues for 2AFC sound lateralization tasks and thus conclude that, at least to broadband clicks, rats show ITD sensitivity.
evidence: This cites a previous study by the authors demonstrating ITD sensitivity in normal hearing rats.

claim: Recent studies in CI patients with late deafness in adults and children have shown that ITDs delivered to mid- and high-frequency cochlear regions can be detected behaviorally.
source: Recent studies in CI patients with late deafness in adults and children have shown that ITDs delivered to mid- and high-frequency cochlear regions can be detected behaviorally (Kan et al., 2016; Ehlers et al., 2017).
evidence: This cites recent clinical studies showing ITD detection in mid- and high-frequency regions.

claim: Electrophysiology studies on congenitally deaf CI cats reported a substantially reduced ITD sensitivity relative to wild-type, hearing experienced cats acutely deafened as adults.
source: Second, electrophysiology studies on congenitally deaf CI cats reported a substantially reduced ITD sensitivity relative to wild-type, hearing experienced cats acutely deafened as adults (Tillein et al., 2010; Hancock et al., 2010; Tillein et al., 2016).
evidence: This cites previous electrophysiology studies in cats for comparison.

claim: In the IC of ND rats, significant ITD sensitivity was found in 91% of recording sites, compared to only 48% reported for congenitally deaf cats or 62% for ND rabbits.
source: In the IC of our ND rats, we found significant ITD sensitivity in 91% of recordings sites, compared to only 48% reported for congenitally deaf cats (Hancock et al., 2010) or 62% for ND rabbits (Chung et al., 2019).
evidence: This compares the proportion of ITD-sensitive sites across species and studies.

claim: When tested under optimal stimulation to deliver microsecond precise ITD cues in a naive auditory system, the proportion of ITD-sensitive sites in NDCI-E rats is more similar to proportions in adult deafened CI-stimulated cats (84–86%), rabbits (~75%), or gerbils (~74%).
source: When tested under optimal stimulation to deliver microsecond precise ITD cues in a naive auditory system, the proportion of ITD-sensitive sites in NDCI-E rats is thus more similar to proportions in adult deafened CI-stimulated cats (84–86%; Smith and Delgutte, 2007; Hancock et al., 2010), rabbits (~75%; Chung et al., 2016; Chung et al., 2019), or gerbils (~74%; Vollmer, 2018).
evidence: This compares the proportion of ITD-sensitive sites with multiple previous studies across species.

claim: It is unknown how much ITD tuning in the IC or AC is necessary to make behavioral ITD discrimination thresholds of ≈50 µs possible.
source: It is important to remember that it is unknown how much ITD tuning in the IC or AC is necessary, or whether this is species specific, to make behavioral ITD discrimination thresholds of ≈50 µs possible, as we see in our NDCI-B cohort (Figure 2).
evidence: This identifies a gap in understanding the relationship between neural and behavioral ITD sensitivity.

claim: Multi-units with STVRs in the range reported for congenital deaf cats can change their firing rates substantially between steps of only 20 µs ITD.
source: However, multi-units such as #3 and #4 shown in Figure 3 change their firing rates as a function of ITD substantially between steps of only 20 µs. These multi-units have STVRs that are not outside the range reported for congenital deaf cats.
evidence: This is an observation from the electrophysiology data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The level of physiological ITD sensitivity previously observed in cats and rabbits could be sufficient to enable good behavioral ITD discrimination performance if these animals could be trained and tested on an appropriate task.
source: The level of physiological ITD sensitivity previously observed in cats (Tillein et al., 2010; Hancock et al., 2010; Tillein et al., 2016) and rabbits (Chung et al., 2019) could be sufficient to enable good behavioral ITD discrimination performance if only these animals could be trained and tested on an appropriate task.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on comparing physiological sensitivity across species.

claim: Previously reported reductions in physiological ITD sensitivity in the IC or AC of early deaf animals do not seem large enough to fully explain the very poor behavioral ITD thresholds seen in most early deaf humans.
source: Thus, in our opinion, any previously reported reductions in physiological ITD sensitivity seen in the IC (Chung et al., 2016; Chung et al., 2019) or AC (Tillein et al., 2010; Tillein et al., 2016) of early deaf animals does not seem nearly large enough to fully explain the very poor behavioral ITD thresholds seen in most early deaf humans.
evidence: This is an inference comparing animal physiology data with human behavioral outcomes.

claim: The behavioral ITD sensitivity of NDCI-B rats compares favorably with that in NH-B animals, suggesting that the poor ITD sensitivity in human CI patients may have causes beyond the lack of auditory experience during a presumed critical period.
source: And indeed, our own findings that the behavioral ITD sensitivity of our NDCI-B rats compares favorably with that in NH-B animals strongly suggests that the poor ITD sensitivity in human CI patients may well have causes beyond the lack of auditory experience during a presumed critical period.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the behavioral results.

claim: It is unclear why congenitally deaf cats show a modest reduction in neural ITD sensitivity, while NDCI-E rats in the present study seem not to.
source: It is unclear why congenitally deaf cats (Hancock et al., 2010; Hancock et al., 2013) show a modest reduction in neural ITD sensitivity, while NDCI-E rats in the present study seem not to.
evidence: This acknowledges uncertainty about species differences in the results.

claim: Both congenitally deaf cats and NDCI-E rats exhibit a lot of innate residual ITD sensitivity in their midbrains despite severe hearing impairment throughout their development.
source: More pertinent for the present discussion is that both preparations exhibit a lot of innate residual ITD sensitivity in their midbrains despite severe hearing impairment throughout their development (Tillein et al., 2010; Hancock et al., 2010; Hancock et al., 2013; Tillein et al., 2016; Chung et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a synthesis of findings across multiple studies including the current one.

claim: With appropriate rehabilitation and training, neonatally deaf cats and rabbits (and perhaps even humans) might be able to learn to make use of their residual innate physiological ITD sensitivity to perform very well in binaural hearing tasks.
source: Thus, in light of our new behavioral results in rats, it seems reasonable to expect that, with appropriate rehabilitation and training, neonatally deaf cats and rabbits (and perhaps even humans) might be able to learn to make use of their residual innate physiological ITD sensitivity to perform very well in binaural hearing tasks.
evidence: This is a speculative extrapolation from the rat behavioral results to other species.

claim: The most striking difference between the current results and other previously published work is that the behavioral ITD discrimination thresholds of NDCI-B rats are an order of magnitude or more better than those of early deaf human CI patients.
source: The most striking difference between our results and other previously published work remains that the behavioral ITD discrimination thresholds of our NDCI-B rats are an order of magnitude or more better than those of early deaf human CI patients (Gordon et al., 2014; Litovsky and Gordon, 2016; Ehlers et al., 2017).
evidence: This compares the current behavioral results with published human data.

claim: Previous authors have proposed that the very poor performance typical of early deaf human CI patients may be due to lack of early exposure to consistent timing differences between the ears.
source: As mentioned in the introduction, previous authors have proposed that the very poor performance typical of early deaf human CI patients may be due to 'factors such as auditory deprivation, in particular, lack of early exposure to consistent timing differences between the ears' (Ehlers et al., 2017), in other words, the critical period hypothesis.
evidence: This cites a previous hypothesis about the cause of poor ITD sensitivity in early deaf CI patients.

claim: Neonatal deafening and severe hearing loss until reaching developmental maturity did not prevent NDCI-B rats from achieving very good ITD discrimination performance.
source: However, neonatal deafening and severe hearing loss until reaching developmental maturity did not prevent our NDCI-B rats from achieving very good ITD discrimination performance.
evidence: This is a summary of the behavioral findings.

claim: The current results on early deafened CI rats show that lack of auditory input during early development does not need to result in poor ITD sensitivity and is therefore unlikely to be a sufficient explanation for the poor ITD sensitivity found in early deaf CI patients.
source: Nevertheless, our results on early deafened CI rats show that lack of auditory input during early development does not need to result in poor ITD sensitivity and is therefore unlikely to be a sufficient explanation for the poor ITD sensitivity found in early deaf CI patients.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results about the critical period hypothesis.

claim: Most developmental studies of the binaural circuitry in animal models have focused on low-frequency fine-structure ITD pathways through the MSO, rather than LSO envelope ITD pathways.
source: Most of these studies have focused on low-frequency fine-structure ITD pathways through the MSO, rather than lateral superior olive (LSO) envelope ITD pathways that are likely to be of particular relevance for the CI ITD processing we are studying here.
evidence: This is a characterization of the focus of previous developmental studies.

claim: Developmental studies in ferrets have shown that the formation of afferent synapses to MSO is essentially complete before the onset of hearing.
source: For example, developmental studies in ferrets have shown that the formation of afferent synapses to MSO, one of the main brainstem nuclei for ITD processing, is essentially complete before the onset of hearing (Brunso-Bechtold et al., 1992).
evidence: This cites a developmental study in ferrets showing early maturation of MSO synapses.

claim: In mice, the highly specialized calyxes of Held synapses mature before the onset of hearing.
source: In mice, the highly specialized calyxes of Held synapses, which are thought to play key roles in relaying precisely timed information in the binaural circuitry, have been shown to mature before the onset of hearing (Hoffpauir et al., 2006).
evidence: This cites a developmental study in mice showing early maturation of calyxes of Held.

claim: In gerbils, key parts of the binaural ITD processing circuitry in the auditory brainstem will fail to mature when driven with strong, uninformative omnidirectional white noise stimulation during development.
source: For example, in gerbils, key parts of the binaural ITD processing circuitry in the auditory brainstem will fail to mature when driven with strong, uninformative omnidirectional white noise stimulation during development (Kapfer et al., 2002; Seidl and Grothe, 2005)
evidence: This cites studies showing that inappropriate sensory input can disturb binaural pathway development.

claim: Tirko and Ryugo, 2012 showed that inhibitory pathways in the MSO are significantly reduced in congenitally deaf cats at postnatal day 90, but can be fully restored with the advent of CI stimulation after only 3 months.
source: A perhaps related finding by Tirko and Ryugo, 2012 shows that inhibitory pathways in the MSO, which are thought to be essential for ITD encoding, are significantly reduced in congenitally deaf cats at postnatal day 90, compared to NH peers, but they can be fully restored with the advent of CI stimulation after only 3 months.
evidence: This cites a study showing reversibility of developmental changes with CI stimulation.

claim: Pecka et al., 2008 demonstrated the importance of glycinergic inhibition and its timing in the MSO in controlling binaural excitation by fine tuning the delay between arrival from the two ears.
source: Finally, Pecka et al., 2008 demonstrated the importance of glycinergic inhibition and its timing in the MSO in controlling binaural excitation by fine tuning the delay between arrival from the two ears, which could allow ITD pathways to be 'tuned', possibly in an experience dependent manner.
evidence: This cites a study on the role of inhibition in ITD processing.

claim: None of the published articles point to a biological mechanism for a critical period that could explain the loss of ITD sensitivity in early deaf CI users merely as a consequence of an absence of input in early life.
source: None of the published articles we could find point to a biological mechanism for a critical period that could explain the loss of ITD sensitivity in early deaf CI users merely as a consequence of an absence of input in early life.
evidence: This is an assessment of the literature regarding mechanisms for critical periods.

claim: The normal auditory system not only combines ITD information with ILD and monaural spectral cues to localize sounds in space, it also adapts strongly to changes in these cues, and can re-weight them depending on their reliability.
source: It is well known that the normal auditory system not only combines ITD information with ILD and monaural spectral cues to localize sounds in space, it also adapts strongly to changes in these cues, and can re-weight them depending on their reliability (Keating et al., 2013b; Keating et al., 2015; Tillein et al., 2016; Kumpik et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations and represents established knowledge about auditory plasticity.

claim: Jones et al., 2011 demonstrated changes in ITD and ILD thresholds as head size and pinnae grow for up to 6 weeks postnatally in chinchillas.
source: Similarly, Jones et al., 2011 demonstrated changes in ITD and ILD thresholds as head size and pinnae grow for up to 6 weeks postnatally in chinchillas.
evidence: This cites a study showing developmental changes in binaural sensitivity.

claim: No studies have demonstrated that critical periods in the ITD pathways will irrevocably close if sensory input is simply absent, rather than altered.
source: However, no studies have demonstrated that critical periods in the ITD pathways will irrevocably close if sensory input is simply absent, rather than altered.
evidence: This is an assessment of what has not been demonstrated in the literature.

claim: By using the rat model, which allowed behavioral study of ITD sensitivity, the authors were able to show conclusively that the ability to use ITD cues perceptually does not disappear permanently after hearing loss during a presumed critical period.
source: By using the rat model, which allowed us to study ITD sensitivity behaviorally, we were able to show conclusively that the ability to use ITD cues perceptually does not disappear permanently after hearing loss during a presumed critical period.
evidence: This is a summary of the main conclusion from the behavioral experiments.

claim: An innate ITD sensitivity could conceivably degrade over the course of prolonged exposure to the entirely inconsistent and uninformative ITDs delivered by current standard clinical CI processors.
source: One possibility that we believe has not been given enough attention is that an innate ITD sensitivity could conceivably degrade over the course of prolonged exposure to the entirely inconsistent and uninformative ITDs delivered by current standard clinical CI processors.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis proposed by the authors as an alternative explanation.

claim: Zheng et al., 2015 and Litovsky and Gordon, 2016 noted that even after binaural CI listening experience extending for >4 years or >6 years, respectively, the ITD sensitivity of bilateral CI users still lags well behind that of age-matched controls with NH.
source: This possibility is consistent with the observations by Zheng et al., 2015 and by Litovsky and Gordon, 2016 who note that, even after binaural CI listening experience extending for >4 years or >6 years, respectively, the ITD sensitivity of bilateral CI users still lags well behind that of age-matched controls with NH.
evidence: This cites observations from clinical studies that are consistent with the maladaptive plasticity hypothesis.

claim: NDCI-B rats received only highly precise and informative ITDs right from the start with no additional auditory cues, and were able to lateralize ITDs as well as their NH litter mates after only 2 weeks of training.
source: Contrast this with our NDCI-B rats, which received only highly precise and informative ITDs right from the start with no additional auditory cues, and were able to lateralize ITDs as well as their NH litter mates after only 2 weeks of training.
evidence: This summarizes the behavioral training results and contrasts them with clinical outcomes.

claim: Clinical CI processors are designed first and foremost for the purpose of delivering all important speech formant information in real life settings, and optimizing ITD coding was not a priority in their original design.
source: Clincal CI processors are, for good reason, designed first and foremost for the purpose of delivering all important speech formant information in real life settings, and optimizing ITD coding was not a priority in their original design.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the design priorities of clinical CI processors.

claim: The current results raise the possibility that incorporating better ITD encoding in clinical processors might lead to better binaural outcomes for future generations of CI patients.
source: Nevertheless, our results raise the possibility that incorporating better ITD encoding in clinical processors might lead to better binaural outcomes for future generations of CI patients.
evidence: This is a speculative inference about potential clinical implications of the findings.

claim: Current CI processors produce pulsatile stimulation based on fixed rate interleaved sampling, which is neither synchronized to stimulus fine structure nor synchronized between ears.
source: Current CI processors produce pulsatile stimulation based on fixed rate interleaved sampling (Wilson et al., 1991; Stupak et al., 2018), which is neither synchronized to stimulus fine structure nor synchronized between ears.
evidence: This describes limitations of current CI technology, supported by citations.

claim: At typical clinical stimulation rates (>900 pps), CI users are not sensitive to speech envelope ITDs, as envelope ITD sensitivity requires peak shaped envelopes.
source: Furthermore, at typical clinical stimulation rates (>900 pps), CI users are not sensitive to speech envelope ITDs, as envelope ITD sensitivity requires peak shaped envelopes (Laback et al., 2004; Grantham et al., 2008; van Hoesel et al., 2009; Noel and Eddington, 2013; Laback et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations documenting limitations of envelope ITD sensitivity at high pulse rates.

claim: Speech processors only ever provide uninformative envelope ITDs to the children using them because the carrier pulses are too fast and the envelope shapes in everyday sounds are not peaked enough.
source: Consequently, the carrier pulses are too fast, and the envelope shapes in everyday sounds are not peaked enough, so that speech processors only ever provide uninformative envelope ITDs to the children using them (Laback et al., 2004; Grantham et al., 2008; Laback et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited limitations of CI technology.

claim: Brainstem circuits of children fitted with conventional bilateral CIs may 'learn' to ignore the unhelpful ITDs contained in the inputs they receive.
source: Perhaps brainstem circuits of children fitted with conventional bilateral CIs simply 'learn' to ignore the unhelpful ITDs that are contained in the inputs they receive.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis about maladaptive plasticity.

claim: Precise ITD cues at low pulse rates were essentially the only form of useful auditory input that NDCI-B rats experienced, and they quickly learned to use these precise ITD cues.
source: In contrast, precise ITD cues at low pulse rates were essentially the only form of useful auditory input that our NDCI-B rats experienced, and they quickly learned to use these precise ITD cues.
evidence: This describes the experimental conditions and outcomes for the NDCI-B rats.

claim: The mammalian auditory system may develop ITD sensitivity in the absence of early sensory input and this sensitivity may then be either refined or lost, depending on how informative the binaural inputs turn out to be.
source: Thus, our data raise the possibility that the mammalian auditory system may develop ITD sensitivity in the absence of early sensory input and that this sensitivity may then be either refined or lost, depending on how informative the binaural inputs turn out to be.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis based on the experimental results.

claim: The inability of early deaf CI patients to use ITDs may be somewhat similar to conditions such as amblyopia or failures of stereoscopic depth vision development, which are caused more by unbalanced or inappropriate inputs than by a lack of sensory experience.
source: The inability of early deaf CI patients to use ITDs may thus be somewhat similar to conditions such as amblyopia or failures of stereoscopic depth vision development, pathologies that are caused more by unbalanced or inappropriate inputs than by a lack of sensory experience (Levi et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a speculative analogy drawn between auditory and visual critical period phenomena.

claim: For the visual system, it has been shown that orientation selective neuronal responses exist at eye-opening and thus are established without visual input.
source: For the visual system, it has been shown that orientation selective neuronal responses exist at eye-opening and thus are established without visual input (Ko et al., 2013).
evidence: This cites a study showing innate visual processing capabilities.

claim: It may be possible to 'protect' ITD sensitivity in young bilateral CI users by exposing them to regular periods of precise ITD information from the beginning of binaural stimulation.
source: If this hypothesis is correct, then it may be possible to 'protect' ITD sensitivity in young bilateral CI users by exposing them to regular periods of precise ITD information from the beginning of binaural stimulation.
evidence: This is a speculative proposal for clinical intervention based on the hypothesis.

claim: Whether CI patients are able to recover normal ITD sensitivity much later if rehabilitated with useful ITDs for prolonged periods, or whether their ability to process microsecond ITDs atrophies irreversibly, is unknown and will require further investigation.
source: Whether CI patients are able to recover normal ITD sensitivity much later if rehabilitated with useful ITDs for prolonged periods, or whether their ability to process microsecond ITDs atrophies irreversibly, is unknown and will require further investigation.
evidence: This identifies an open question for future research.

claim: The CIS paradigm times the stimulus pulses so that only one electrode channel delivers a pulse at any one time, which has been shown to minimize cross-channel interactions due to 'current spread'.
source: The CIS paradigm (Wilson et al., 1991) from which most processor algorithms are derived times the stimulus pulses, so that only one electrode channel delivers a pulse at any one time. This has been shown to minimize cross-channel interactions due to 'current spread' which might compromise the already quite limited tonotopic place coding of CIs.
evidence: This describes a feature of CIS processing and its rationale, supported by citation.

claim: CI processors run at high pulse rates (≥900 Hz), which may be necessary to encode sufficient amplitude modulations for speech recognition.
source: Additionally, CI processors run at high pulse rates (≥900 Hz), which may be necessary to encode sufficient amplitude modulations for speech recognition (Loizou et al., 2000).
evidence: This describes another feature of CI processing and its rationale, supported by citation.

claim: ITD discrimination has been shown to deteriorate when pulse rates exceeded a few hundred Hz in humans and animals.
source: However, ITD discrimination has been shown to deteriorate when pulse rates exceeded a few hundred Hz in humans (van Hoesel, 2007; Laback et al., 2007) and animals (Joris and Yin, 1998; Chung et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies showing rate limitations on ITD sensitivity.

claim: The behavioral experiments described in this study were conducted with low pulse rates (50 Hz).
source: Our own behavioral experiments described here were conducted with low pulse rates (50 Hz)
evidence: This describes a parameter of the experimental design.

claim: Future work will need to determine whether ITD discrimination performance declines at higher pulse rates.
source: and future work will need to determine whether ITD discrimination performance declines at higher pulse rates which would make pulse rate an important factor for the development of good ITD sensitivity under this stimulation conditions.
evidence: This identifies a limitation and direction for future research.

claim: Promising research is underway to improve ITD coding in CI processors, including providing fine structure information on apical electrodes, using a mixture of different pulse rates for different electrode channels, presenting redundant temporal fine structure information to multiple electrode channels, or introducing occasional 'double pulses' into the stimulus.
source: While difficult, this may not be impossible, and promising, research is underway, which either provides fine structure information on up to four apical electrodes while running CIS strategy on the remaining electrodes (MED-EL CIs; Riss et al., 2014), uses a mixture of different pulse rates for different electrode channels (Thakkar et al., 2018), presents redundant temporal fine structure information to multiple electrode channels (Churchill et al., 2014), or aims to 'reset' the brain's ITD extraction mechanisms by introducing occasional 'double pulses' into the stimulus (Srinivasan et al., 2018).
evidence: This cites multiple ongoing research efforts to improve ITD coding in CIs.

claim: The current results underscore the need to pursue research on improved ITD coding with urgency as evidence has been provided that the absence of auditory input during a critical period does not necessarily mean that early deafened CI users show poor or no ITD sensitivity.
source: Our results underscore the need to pursue this work with urgency as we have provided evidence that the absence of auditory input during a critical period does not necessarily mean that early deafened CI users show poor or no ITD sensitivity.
evidence: This is an inference about the implications of the findings for future research priorities.

claim: While the 'maladaptive plasticity hypothesis' is compatible with the experimental data presented, it has not been proven correct and is just one possible alternative explanation for the observed poor ITD sensitivity of human bilateral CI users.
source: On a final note, we would be remiss if we did not acknowledge that, while the 'maladaptive plasticity hypothesis' that we have elaborated over the last few paragraphs is 'compatible' with the experimental data we have presented, it would be wrong to assert that our data so far prove that this hypothesis is correct. At present, we have merely managed to shed serious doubts on the popular critical period hypothesis, but at present, the maladaptive plasticity hypothesis is still, apart from others including different etiologies of deafness, just one possible alternative explanation for the observed poor ITD sensitivity of human bilateral CI users.
evidence: This is a cautious acknowledgment of the limitations of the current study in proving the maladaptive plasticity hypothesis.

claim: The maladaptive plasticity hypothesis still needs to be put to the test by measuring the effect of deliberately degrading the quality of ITD cues to varying extent and over various periods.
source: It still needs to be put to the test by measuring the effect of deliberately degrading the quality of ITD cues to varying extent and over various periods.
evidence: This identifies a specific experimental approach needed to test the hypothesis.

claim: The animal model introduced in this study makes testing the maladaptive plasticity hypothesis experimentally feasible.
source: However, the animal model introduced in this study now makes this important task experimentally feasible.
evidence: This is a claim about the utility of the developed animal model for future research.

claim: All procedures involving experimental animals reported in this study were approved by the Department of Health of Hong Kong and/or the Regierungspräsidium Freiburg, as well as by the appropriate local ethical review committee.
source: All procedures involving experimental animals reported here were approved by the Department of Health of Hong Kong (#16–52 DH/HA and P/8/2/5) and/or the Regierungspräsidium Freiburg (#35–9185.81/G-17/124), as well as by the appropriate local ethical review committee.
evidence: This is a statement about ethical approval for the research.

claim: A total of 14 rats were obtained for this study from the breeding facilities of the Chinese University of Hong Kong or from Janvier Labs.
source: A total of 14 rats were obtained for this study from the breeding facilities of the Chinese University of Hong Kong or from Janvier Labs (Le Genest-Saint-Isle, France), and these were allocated randomly to the deafened and hearing experienced cohorts described in Figure 1.
evidence: This describes the source and allocation of experimental animals.

claim: Rats were deafened by daily intraperitoneal injections of 400 mg/kg kanamycin from postnatal days 9 to 20 inclusively.
source: Rats were deafened by daily intraperitoneal (i.p.) injections of 400 mg/kg kanamycin from postnatal days 9 to 20 inclusively (Osako et al., 1979; Rosskothen-Kuhl and Illing, 2012).
evidence: This describes the deafening protocol used in the study.

claim: The kanamycin treatment is known to cause widespread death of inner and outer hair cells while keeping the number of spiral ganglion cells comparable to that in untreated control rats.
source: This is known to cause widespread death of inner and outer hair cells (Osako et al., 1979; Matsuda et al., 1999; Argence et al., 2008) while keeping the number of spiral ganglion cells comparable to that in untreated control rats (Osako et al., 1979; Argence et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies characterizing the effects of kanamycin treatment.

claim: Rat pups treated with kanamycin achieve hearing thresholds around 70 dB for only a short period (~p14–16) and are severely to profoundly hearing impaired thereafter.
source: Osako et al., 1979 have shown that rat pups treated with this method achieve hearing thresholds around 70 dB for only a short period (~p14–16) and are severely to profoundly hearing impaired thereafter
evidence: This cites a previous study characterizing the time course of hearing loss with this deafening method.

claim: The kanamycin deafening procedure results in widespread disturbances in the histological development of central auditory pathways, including a nearly complete loss of tonotopic organization.
source: resulting in widespread disturbances in the histological development of their central auditory pathways, including a nearly complete loss of tonotopic organization (Rosskothen-Kuhl and Illing, 2012; Rauch et al., 2016; Rosskothen-Kuhl et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies characterizing central effects of neonatal deafening.

claim: Profound hearing loss (>90 dB) was verified by the loss of Preyer's reflex, the absence of ABRs to broadband click stimuli as well as pure tones, and by performing histological assessment on cochlea sections.
source: We verified that this procedure provoked profound hearing loss (>90 dB) by the loss of Preyer's reflex (Jero et al., 2001), the absence of ABRs to broadband click stimuli (Figure 5b) as well as pure tones (at 500, 1000, 2000, and 8000 Hz), and by performing histological assessment on cochlea sections of 11 weeks old, ND rats (data not shown).
evidence: This describes the methods used to verify deafness in the experimental animals.

claim: Normal rats typically exhibited click ABR thresholds near 30 dB SPL.
source: While normal rats typically exhibited click ABR thresholds near 30 dB SPL (Figure 5a)
evidence: This describes the normal hearing thresholds observed in control rats, shown in Figure 5a.

claim: Deafened rats had very high click thresholds of ≥130 dB SPL.
source: deafened rats had very high click thresholds of ≥130 dB SPL (Figure 5b).
evidence: This describes the elevated hearing thresholds in deafened rats, shown in Figure 5b.

claim: All animals were implanted in early adulthood (between 10 and 14 weeks postnatally) for both behavioral training and electrophysiology recordings.
source: All animals were implanted in early adulthood (between 10 and 14 weeks postnatally) for both behavioral training and electrophysiology recordings (Figure 1).
evidence: This describes the timing of CI implantation in the experimental animals.

claim: Two to four rings of an eight-channel electrode carrier were fully inserted through a cochleostomy in medio-dorsal direction into the middle turn of both cochleae.
source: In short, two to four rings of an eight-channel electrode carrier (Cochlear Ltd animal array ST08.45, Cochlear Ltd, Peira, Beerse, Belgium) were fully inserted through a cochleostomy in medio-dorsal direction into the middle turn of both cochleae.
evidence: This describes the surgical procedure for CI implantation.

claim: Electrically evoked ABRs were measured for each ear individually to verify that both CIs were successfully implanted and operated at acceptably low electrical stimulation thresholds, usually around 100 μA.
source: Electrically evoked ABRs (EABRs) were measured for each ear individually to verify that both CIs were successfully implanted and operated at acceptably low electrical stimulation thresholds, usually around 100 μA with a duty cycle of 61.44 µs positive, 40.96 µs at zero, and 61.44 µs negative (Figure 5c).
evidence: This describes the verification of successful CI implantation using EABRs.

claim: The electrical stimuli used biphasic current pulses similar to those used in clinical devices with a duty cycle of 61.44 µs positive, 40.96 µs at zero, 61.44 µs negative.
source: All electrical intracochlear stimulation used biphasic current pulses similar to those used in clinical devices (duty cycle: 61.44 µs positive, 40.96 µs at zero, 61.44 µs negative)
evidence: This describes the electrical stimulation parameters used in the study.

claim: For behavioral training, all NDCI-B rats were stimulated 6 dB above threshold.
source: For behavioral training, we stimulated all NDCI-B rats 6 dB above these thresholds.
evidence: This describes the stimulation intensity used for behavioral training.

claim: Acoustic stimuli used to measure behavioral ITD sensitivity in NH-B rats consisted of a single sample pulse at a sample rate of 48,000 Hz.
source: Acoustic stimuli used to measure behavioral ITD sensitivity in NH-B rats consisted of a single sample pulse (generated as a digital delta function 'click') at a sample rate of 48,000 Hz.
evidence: This describes the acoustic stimulation parameters for normal hearing rats.

claim: Acoustic stimuli were delivered at sound intensities of ≈80 dB SPL.
source: Stimuli were delivered at sound intensities of ≈80 dB SPL.
evidence: This describes the intensity of acoustic stimulation.

claim: A 3D printed 'rat acoustical manikin' with miniature microphones in each ear canal was used for validating that the acoustic setup delivered the desired ITDs and no usable intensity cues.
source: A 3D printed 'rat acoustical manikin' with miniature microphones in each ear canal was used for validating that the acoustic setup delivered the desired ITDs and no usable intensity cues (see Figure 2—figure supplement 2 and Li et al., 2019).
evidence: This describes the validation method for the acoustic stimulation setup.

claim: The residual ILDs in the acoustic setup are much smaller than the reported behavioral thresholds for ferrets (~1.3 dB) or rats (~3 dB).
source: Note that the residual ILDs are much smaller than the reported behavioral thresholds for ferrets (~1.3 dB Keating et al., 2014) or rats (~3 dB Wesolek et al., 2010).
evidence: This compares the residual ILDs in the setup with published behavioral thresholds to show they are not informative.

claim: ITDs could be varied in steps of 20.48 µs for the electrical stimuli and 20.83 µs for the acoustic stimuli.
source: Given the sample rates of the devices used, ITDs could thus be varied in steps of 20.48 µs for the electrical stimuli and 20.83 µs for the acoustic stimuli.
evidence: This describes the ITD resolution of the stimulation systems.

claim: The behavioral animals were put on a schedule with 6 days of testing followed by 1 day off with ad lib water.
source: The behavioral animals were put on a schedule with 6 days of testing, during which the rats obtained their drinking water as a positive reinforcer, followed by 1 day off, with ad lib water.
evidence: This describes the water restriction schedule used for behavioral training.

claim: During testing periods, the rats were given two sessions per day, each lasting 25–30 min, which typically took 150–200 trials during which ≈10 ml of water were consumed.
source: During testing periods, the rats were given two sessions per day. Each session lasted 25–30 min, which typically took 150–200 trials during which ≈10 ml of water were consumed.
evidence: This describes the behavioral testing schedule and water consumption.

claim: Correct lateralization triggered three drops of water as positive reinforcement, while incorrect responses triggered no water delivery but caused a 5–15 s timeout.
source: Correct lateralization triggered three drops of water as positive reinforcement. Incorrect responses triggered no water delivery but caused a 5–15 s timeout during which no new trial could be initiated.
evidence: This describes the reinforcement contingencies in the behavioral task.

claim: The NDCI-B rats received a flashing LED as negative feedback stimulus instead of a negative feedback sound to avoid potential discomfort from prolonged negative feedback stimuli.
source: Given that CI stimulation can be experienced as effortful by human patients (Perreau et al., 2017), and to avoid potential discomfort from prolonged negative feedback stimuli, the NDCI-B rats received a flashing LED as an alternative negative feedback stimulus.
evidence: This describes a methodological choice to minimize discomfort in CI-stimulated rats.

claim: After each correct trial a new ITD was chosen randomly from a set spanning ±160 μs in 25 µs steps, but after each incorrect trial, the last stimulus was repeated in a 'correction trial'.
source: After each correct trial a new ITD was chosen randomly from a set spanning ±160 μs in 25 µs steps, but after each incorrect trial, the last stimulus was repeated in a 'correction trial'.
evidence: This describes the trial structure and correction trial procedure.

claim: Correction trials prevent animals from developing idiosyncratic biases favoring one side but are excluded from the final psychometric performance analysis.
source: Correction trials prevent animals from developing idiosyncratic biases favoring one side (Walker et al., 2009; Keating et al., 2014), but since they could be answered correctly without attention to the stimuli by a simple 'if you just made a mistake, change side' strategy, they are excluded from the final psychometric performance analysis.
evidence: This explains the rationale for correction trials and their exclusion from analysis.

claim: The NH-B rats received their acoustic stimuli through stainless steel hollow ear tubes placed such that the tips were located right next to each ear when the animal was engaging the start spout.
source: The NH-B rats received their acoustic stimuli through stainless steel hollow ear tubes placed such that, when the animal was engaging the start spout, the tips of the tubes were located right next to each ear of the animal to allow near-field stimulation (Figure 2—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: This describes the acoustic stimulus delivery method for NH rats.

claim: The acoustic setup produced a channel separation between ears of ≥20 dB at the lowest, fundamental frequency, and around 40 dB overall.
source: It produced a channel separation between ears of ≥20 dB at the lowest, fundamental frequency, and around 40 dB overall.
evidence: This describes the acoustic isolation achieved by the stimulus delivery system.

claim: Immediately following bilateral CI implantation, anesthetized NDCI-E rats were head fixed in a stereotactic frame and craniotomies were performed bilaterally just anterior to lambda.
source: Immediately following bilateral CI implantation, anesthetized NDCI-E rats were head fixed in a stereotactic frame (RWD Life Sciences), craniotomies were performed bilaterally just anterior to lambda.
evidence: This describes the surgical preparation for electrophysiology recordings.

claim: A single-shaft, 32-channel silicon electrode array was inserted stereotactically into the left or right IC through the overlying occipital cortex.
source: A single-shaft, 32-channel silicon electrode array (ATLAS Neuroengineering, E32-50-S1-L6) was inserted stereotactically into the left or right IC through the overlying occipital cortex using a micromanipulator (RWD Life Sciences).
evidence: This describes the electrode insertion procedure for IC recordings.

claim: Extracellular signals were sampled at a rate of 24.414 kHz with a TDT RZ2 with a NeuroDigitizer head-stage and BrainWare software.
source: Extracellular signals were sampled at a rate of 24.414 kHz with a TDT RZ2 with a NeuroDigitizer head-stage and BrainWare software.
evidence: This describes the data acquisition system for electrophysiology recordings.

claim: The IC recordings typically exhibited short response latencies (≈ 3–5 ms), which suggests that they may come predominantly from the central region of IC.
source: Our recordings typically exhibited short response latencies (≈ 3–5 ms), which suggests that they may come predominantly from the central region of IC.
evidence: This is an inference about the anatomical source of the recordings based on response latencies.

claim: ITD tuning curves were measured by presenting single pulse binaural stimuli with equal amplitude in each ear, ≈10 dB above the contralateral ear threshold, in pseudo-random order.
source: We then measured ITD tuning curves by presenting single pulse binaural stimuli with equal amplitude in each ear, ≈10 dB above the contralateral ear threshold, in pseudo-random order.
evidence: This describes the stimulation protocol for measuring ITD tuning curves.

claim: ITDs varied from 163.84 μs contralateral ear leading to 163.84 μs ipsilateral ear leading in 20.48 μs steps, with each ITD value presented 30 times at each recording site.
source: ITDs varied from 163.84 μs contralateral ear leading to 163.84 μs ipsilateral ear leading in 20.48 μs steps. Each ITD value was presented 30 times at each recording site.
evidence: This describes the ITD range and number of repetitions for electrophysiology measurements.

claim: The inter-stimulus interval for electrophysiology recordings was 500 ms.
source: The inter-stimulus interval was 500 ms.
evidence: This describes the timing between stimuli in the electrophysiology experiments.

claim: At the end of the recording session, the animals were overdosed with pentobarbitone.
source: At the end of the recording session, the animals were overdosed with pentobarbitone.
evidence: This describes the euthanasia procedure at the end of electrophysiology experiments.

claim: The average activity for each stimulus was calculated over a response period (3–80 ms post-stimulus onset) as well as baseline activity (300–500 ms after stimulus onset) at each electrode position.
source: To quantify the extracellular multi-unit responses, we calculated the average activity for each stimulus over a response period (3–80 ms post-stimulus onset) as well as baseline activity (300–500 ms after stimulus onset) at each electrode position.
evidence: This describes the analysis method for quantifying neural responses.

claim: The first 2.5 ms post-stimulus onset was dominated by electrical stimulus artifacts and were discarded.
source: The first 2.5 ms post-stimulus onset was dominated by electrical stimulus artifacts and were discarded.
evidence: This describes a data processing step to remove stimulus artifacts.

claim: Multi-unit spikes were extracted by simple threshold crossings of the band-passed (300 Hz–6 kHz) electrode signal with a threshold set at 4 standard deviations of the signal amplitude.
source: For display purposes of the raster plots in Figure 3, we extracted multi-unit spikes by simple threshold crossings of the band-passed (300 Hz–6 kHz) electrode signal with a threshold set at 4 standard deviation of the signal amplitude.
evidence: This describes the spike detection method for creating raster plots.

claim: To quantify responses for tuning curves, an analog measure of multi-unit activity (AMUA) amplitudes was computed by band-passing (300 Hz–6 kHz), rectifying, and low-passing (6 kHz) the electrode signal.
source: To quantify responses for tuning curves, instead of counting spikes by threshold crossings, we instead computed an analog measure of multi-unit activity (AMUA) amplitudes as described in Schnupp et al., 2015. The mean AMUA amplitude during the response and baseline periods was computed by band-passing (300 Hz–6 kHz), rectifying (taking the absolute value) and low-passing (6 kHz) the electrode signal.
evidence: This describes the AMUA analysis method for quantifying neural responses.

claim: The AMUA measure gives a less noisy measure of multi-unit neural activity than counting spikes by conventional threshold crossing measures.
source: This AMUA value thus measures the mean signal amplitude in the frequency range in which spikes have energy. As illustrated in Figure 1 of Schnupp et al., 2015, this gives a less noisy measure of multi-unit neural activity than counting spikes by conventional threshold crossing measures because the latter are subject to errors due to spike collisions, noise events, or small spikes sometimes reach threshold and sometimes not.
evidence: This explains the rationale for using AMUA, supported by citation.

claim: STVR values are a measure of the strength of tuning of neural responses to ITD, defined as the proportion of trial-to-trial variance in response amplitude explained by changes in ITD.
source: STVR values are a measure of the strength of tuning of neural responses to ITD, which we adopted from Hancock et al., 2010 to facilitate quantitative comparisons. The STVR is defined in Hancock et al., 2010 as the proportion of trial-to-trial variance in response amplitude explained by changes in ITD.
evidence: This defines the STVR metric used to quantify ITD sensitivity, citing its source.

claim: An STVR > 0.5 is considered good ITD sensitivity.
source: For interpretation purposes, an STVR > 0.5 is considered good ITD sensitivity.
evidence: This provides a criterion for interpreting STVR values.

claim: p<0.01 from ANOVA served as a criterion to determine whether the ITD tuning of a given multi-unit was deemed statistically significant.
source: p-Values were also computed from the one-way ANOVA and p<0.01 served as a criterion to determine whether the ITD tuning of a given multi-unit was deemed statistically significant.
evidence: This describes the statistical criterion for significant ITD tuning.

claim: Psychometric models were fitted to the observed proportions of 'right' responses as a function of stimulus ITD using maximum likelihood estimation.
source: We fitted the model in Equation 2 to the observed proportions of 'right' responses as a function of stimulus ITD using the scipy.optimize.minimize() function of Python 3.4, using gradient descent methods to find maximum likelihood estimates for the parameters α, β, γ, and δ given the data.
evidence: This describes the statistical method for fitting psychometric curves.

claim: The cumulative Gaussian model fitted the behavioral data very well.
source: This cumulative Gaussian model fitted the data very well, as is readily apparent in Figure 2a–j.
evidence: This is an assessment of the goodness of fit of the psychometric model, visible in Figure 2.

claim: The slope of the psychometric function around zero ITD was used as the maximum likelihood estimate of the animal's ITD sensitivity.
source: We then used the slope of the psychometric function around zero ITD as our maximum likelihood estimate of the animal's ITD sensitivity, as plotted in Figure 2k.
evidence: This describes how ITD sensitivity was quantified from the psychometric curves.

claim: Seventy-five percent correct thresholds were computed as the mean absolute ITD at which the psychometric dips below 25% or rises above 75% 'right' responses.
source: Seventy-five percent of correct thresholds were computed as the mean absolute ITD at which the psychometric dips below 25% or rises above 75% 'right' responses, respectively.
evidence: This describes how behavioral thresholds were calculated from the psychometric curves.
